item.title: Types of Equations: A Quick Map from Algebra to Calculus
item.author: hari@dasarpai.com (Dr. Hari Thapliyaal)
item.description:
Types of Equations
#

What you are solving for, and how the unknown appears
#

An equation says two expressions have the same value. You often solve for an unknown number, unknown function, or unknown vector.

Two labels help before the list:

  • Conditional equation — true only for some values. Example: $2x + 3 = 7$ (solution: $x = 2$).
  • Identity — true for every allowed value. Example: $(x + 1)^2 = x^2 + 2x + 1$.

The table below is a family map, not a strict taxonomy. One expression can fit more than one row (a quadratic can also be transcendental if it uses $\sin x$).

Family You usually find One example
Algebraic Numbers in powers and roots $x^2 - 4 = 0$
Differential Functions and their rates of change $\frac{dy}{dx} = ky$
Transcendental Values inside exp, log, trig $2^x = 8$
Functional A whole function $f$ $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y)$
Integral A function under an integral $f(x) = g(x) + \int_a^b K(x,t)f(t),dt$
Parametric A curve via a parameter $t$ $x = \cos t$, $y = \sin t$
Matrix / vector A vector $x$ in $Ax = b$ $2x_1 + x_2 = 5$ and $x_1 + 3x_2 = 7$ (same system as §7)

For how symbols are read in any expression, see The Grammar of Mathematics: Operators, Functions, Relations, and Symbols Explained. For the number sets those symbols use, see Kinds of Numbers: A Map from Natural to Complex.
